claim: Most roots are disyllabic and virtually all begin with a consonant; the two explicitly named vowel-initial exceptions are particles aa and awuuru.

source_forms.initial_classes: all stops, nasals and both semivowels attested root-initially

normalized_environment: root-initial onset normally obligatory; two particle exceptions
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Two explicitly listed vowel-initial particles are exceptions; the source says 'virtually all', not categorically all, roots begin with consonants.
table_figure: initial-consonant frequency table; root template following vowel-cooccurrence discussion

claim: About 45% of roots are vowel-final; consonant-final roots are restricted to sonorant types: rhotics, the lateral, /n/, /nh/, or /y/, with one explicitly identified /w/-final exclamation.
normalized_environment: root-final coda restricted to sonorants; isolated w-final exclamation
scope: roots; percentages based on consonant-final roots
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The exclamation gaw is the sole known w-final root in the source corpus.

claim: Stop voicing is non-contrastive and positionally conditioned: stops tend to be voiceless and unaspirated word-initially and after short vowels, but voiced post-consonantally and after long vowels.
formal_environment: stop realization conditioned by left context and word edge
normalized_environment: STOP -> voiceless unaspirated / #__, Vshort__; voiced / C__, Vlong__ (tendencies)
scope: general phonetic tendency; voicing not phonemic
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The source explicitly uses 'tend to', so this is staged as a gradient allophonic tendency rather than categorical complementary distribution.
section: 2.1 Phonemes and their realizations, immediately before 2.2

claim: In rapid speech, root-/word-initial /d/ following a vowel-final word can surface as a flap or trill, while the underlying /d/ is retained in slow/careful-speech representation.

source_forms.example: bunggu 'knee' + dagaadhi 'sat down' -> bunggurragaadhi 'knelt' in rapid speech

formal_environment: V# d... in rapid connected speech
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The source contrasts this explicitly with slow and careful speech and presents it as a possible pronunciation, not an obligatory categorical rule.

claim: The root corpus shows highly nonuniform vowel frequencies and specific consonant-vowel associations: /i/ is unusually frequent after initial /dy/ but rare after initial /g/ and /ng/, and no n+i initial sequence had been encountered in the corpus.

source_forms.initial_n_i: 0 attested in words so far encountered

normalized_environment: gradient C-V cooccurrence skew, strongest dy+i attraction and g/ng/n+i underrepresentation
scope: working root dictionary; descriptive frequency statement
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The source frames these as frequency effects and says n+i is unattested only in words 'so far encountered'; none should be promoted to a categorical universal.

claim: There is weak statistical evidence for root-internal vowel matching: in disyllabic roots the second vowel matches the first more often than its baseline second-syllable frequency predicts.
formal_environment: V1 C V2 within disyllabic root
normalized_environment: P(V2=V1) modestly exceeds V2 baseline for all three vowels
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Haviland explicitly calls the evidence 'slight' and a 'weak sort of vowel harmony'; mismatching vowels are common and the pattern is not categorical harmony.
table_figure: prose percentages following C-V frequency tables

claim: The syllable has an obligatory non-complex onset and a non-branching coda; the minimal stem is bimoraic, while monosyllabic bimoraic stems are rare (8/731, about 1%).

source_forms.syllable: obligatory single-C onset; at most one coda C

normalized_environment: σ onset=C exactly one; coda<=1C; Stem>=2μ
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Monosyllabic stems are permitted if bimoraic; one listed noun dii 'tea' is a loan. The rarity is empirical, not a categorical disyllabicity requirement.
section: 3 Recursive PrWd structure in Guugu Yimidhirr

claim: Long vowels are categorically restricted to the first and/or second syllable of the stem in the analyzed 731-root corpus; later stem syllables are light.
normalized_environment: Vː -> allowed only in stem syllable 1 or 2
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Compounds may contain long vowels in the first two syllables of each component, showing that the restriction is stem/prosodic-word-domain based rather than a simple absolute word-position ban.
